title: Lying increases trust in science
source: Show notes (DOI link only; no abstract or figures supplied)
one_line: A sociological theory paper arguing that certain forms of misrepresentation or simplification in the public communication of science can, counterintuitively, raise public trust in science.
key_claims: The episode's framing is that lying — in the sense of overstating certainty or smoothing over messiness — can increase rather than erode trust in science.
No supporting numbers, effect sizes, or study samples were available in the material provided for this card.
limitations: The show notes contained only a DOI, so no methods, data, or author-stated limitations could be verified for this card.
As a Theory and Society piece, the argument is likely conceptual rather than an experimental test of trust outcomes, but this could not be confirmed from the supplied material.
open_questions: What empirical design (e.g. randomised message experiments varying stated certainty) would test whether overclaiming raises measured trust?
Does any trust gain persist after audiences learn the simplification was inaccurate?
Which actors and communication contexts does the argument apply to — individual scientists, institutions, or journalists?
